2: ON THE REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC
3: KORTEWEG–DE VRIES EQUATION
4: Anatoli V. Babin 1, Alexei A. Ilyin 2 and Edriss S. Titi 3
5: This paper is dedicated to the memory of Professor Basil Nicolaenko
6: Abstract. In this paper we develop and use successive averaging method s for explaining the regular-
7: ization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg–de Vries (Kd V) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev
8: spaces ˙H s, for s ≥ 0. Speciﬁcally, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous
9: dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the period ic KdV. For the case where the initial data
10: is in L2 we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these so lutions with respect to the initial
11: data as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s, for s ∈ (−1, 0].
12: Keywords: Korteweg–de Vries equation, dispersive equations, averaging met hod, non-
13: linear resonance.
14: MSC: 35B34,35Q53.
15: 1. Introduction
16: This paper is motivated by works on global regularity of solutions of 3 D problems in
17: hydrodynamics (Navier-Stokes or Boussinesq system with periodic boundary conditions)
18: in the presence of fast rotation or strong stratiﬁcation, see, e.g ., [1], [2], [3], [4], [11],
19: [12], [18], [16], [20], [26], and references therein. The results are base d on the presence of
20: high-frequency waves that lead to destructive interference and eﬀectively weaken the non-
21: linearity through time averaging allowing to prove global regularity of solutions for these
22: problems, at the limit of inﬁnite rotation. The above mentioned hydro dynamical problems
23: are rather complicated (Boussinesq system, for example, involves ﬁve unknown functions of
24: three spatial variables and time, the equations are coupled throug h a quadratic nonlinear-
25: ity). Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to apply this averagin g approach to a slightly
26: simpler problem to make these ideas more transparent. Here we con sider the Korteweg–de
27: Vries equation with one spatial variable subjected to periodic bound ary condition. The
28: averaging eﬀects are strong because on high Fourier modes the line ar term generates high-
29: frequency oscillations which weakens the nonlinearity and makes it mild er. In this paper
30: we show connections between the smoothness properties of solut ions of the Korteweg–de
31: Vries (KdV) equation and the algebraic structure of the nonlinear r esonances between the
32: high-frequency oscillations. Our main goal is to make the relations be tween time-averaging
33: eﬀects and smoothness issues more explicit, rather than to obtain global regularity results
34: under minimal restrictions (see, e.g., [5], [7], [14] and the references therein). In particular,
35: our approach and aim are completely diﬀerent than the machinery an d harmonic analysis
36: Date: Submitted: November 3, 2009. Revised: October 22, 2010. T o appear in: Communications in
37: Pure and Applied Mathematics.
38: 1Department of Mathematics, University of California, Irvine, Califo rnia 92697, USA, E-mail:
39: ababine@math.uci.edu
40: 2Keldysh Institute of Applied Mathematics, Russian Academy of Scien ces, Miusskaya Sq. 4, 125047
41: Moscow, Russia, E-mail: ilyin@keldysh.ru
42: 3Department of Mathematics and Department of Mechanical and Ae rospace Engineering, University
43: of California, Irvine, California 92697, USA, E-mail: etiti@math.uci.edu . Also: Department of Computer
44: Science and Applied Mathematics, Weizmann Institute of Science, P.O . Box 26, Rehovot, 76100, Israel,
45: E-mail: edriss.titi@weizmann.ac.il
46: 1
47: 
48: 2 REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION
49: tools that were developed over the past decade and half for invest igating dispersive partial
50: diﬀerential equations (see the discussion and references mention ed below). Moreover, we
51: also remark that the tools and ideas that are developed in this contr ibution can be easily
52: applied to multi-dimensional equations and multi-component systems , a subject of future
53: investigation.
54: It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
55: also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and
56: [16] to show that fast rotation prevents the formation of a ﬁnite t ime singularity in the
57: two-dimensional Burgers system. We will use this warmup toy model, and in particular
58: the approach in [1], to ﬁx ideas and to illustrate in section 2 the averag ing mechanism,
59: which is instrumental in regularizing the solutions and in preventing th e formation of a
60: ﬁnite time singularity for the two-dimensional inviscid Burgers syste m.
61: Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
62: ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
63: problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
64: we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
65: to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
66: reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
67: in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
68: equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
69: it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
70: similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
71: step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
72: estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
73: the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
74: modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
75: estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can
76: be easily adjusted to general multidimensional problems such as tho se mentioned above
77: in hydrodynamic problems. We do not use in our analysis the speciﬁc pr operties of the
78: KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
79: one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
80: use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
81: The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
82: terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
83: two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the
84: relevant well-posedness results. In section 4 we use the Galerkin pr ocedure for proving the
85: global existence in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s >0. In section 5 we use the Contraction
86: Principle to show that the solutions established in section 4 are unique and Lipschitz
87: continuous, with respect to the initial data, in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s ≥ 1/2. A
88: more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the
89: case s = 0 is dealt with separately. Finally, for solutions with initial data in L2 we show
90: the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions, with resp ect to the initial data,
91: as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s for all s ∈ (−1, 0].
92: There is a long history of the KdV equations in the periodical setting. We do not attempt
93: to give here a complete survey of this long history, but we are satisﬁ ed by mentioning,
94: below, some of the key landmark results. First Bourgain [6] proved local well-posedness in
95: L2. We observe that the result of Bourgain also implies global existence for the real valued
96: KdV in L2. Later the local well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s > −1/2, was
97: 
98: REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION 3
99: established for the real and complex valued KdV by Kenig, Ponce, an d Vega [14]. Later
100: global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1/2, was established for the real"}

37: It is known that the KdV equation, either on a torus or on the whole space, is globally well-
38: posed in H s with s ≥ 0, i.e., there exists a unique solution in C([0, T]; H s) for any initial value
39: in H s; see [1,10,12,33]. However, classical time discretizations for the KdV equation, including
40: finite difference methods, splitting methods, discontinuous Galerkin methods, and classical
41: exponential integrators, generally require much higher regularity for the numerical solutions
42: to converge with certain orders, i.e., these methods typically require u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3) and
43: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 6) to have first- and second-order convergence in L2, respectively. The error
44: estimates under these regularity conditions (or stronger conditions) for the above-mentioned
45: classical time discretizations have been established, for example, in [7–9, 16, 17, 21, 25, 27, 32].
46: Such regularity conditions are not mere technical conditions required in the error analysis.
47: When the solution of the KdV equation does not have the required regularity, its numerical
48: approximations by the classical time discretizations generally have reduced order of conver-
49: gence.
50: In practice, the solutions of the KdV equation may be rough due to measurement or
51: randomness of the data [2, 5]. To address the numerical approximation to nonsmooth so-
52: lutions, some low-regularity exponential integrators based on resonance analysis were re-
53: cently developed to relax the regularity requirement in solving nonlinear dispersive equations.
54: Such low-regularity integrators based on resonance analysis were initially introduced by Hof-
55: manov´ a & Schratz [6] and Ostermann & Schratz [18, 20] for solving the KdV equation and
56: the nonlinear Schr¨ odinger (NLS) equation, respectively. In particular, for the KdV equa-
57: tion, the low-regularity integrator proposed in [6] can have first-order convergence in H 1 for
58: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3). Wu & Zhao [30] showed that another method outlined in [6] can have
59: second-order convergence in H γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+4) with γ ≥ 0. In a more recent arti-

16: This paper is motivated by works on global regularity of solutions of 3 D problems in
17: hydrodynamics (Navier-Stokes or Boussinesq system with periodic boundary conditions)
18: in the presence of fast rotation or strong stratiﬁcation, see, e.g ., [1], [2], [3], [4], [11],

20: high-frequency waves that lead to destructive interference and eﬀectively weaken the non-

24: three spatial variables and time, the equations are coupled throug h a quadratic nonlinear-

26: simpler problem to make these ideas more transparent. Here we con sider the Korteweg–de
27: Vries equation with one spatial variable subjected to periodic bound ary condition. The
28: averaging eﬀects are strong because on high Fourier modes the line ar term generates high-
29: frequency oscillations which weakens the nonlinearity and makes it mild er. In this paper
30: we show connections between the smoothness properties of solut ions of the Korteweg–de
31: Vries (KdV) equation and the algebraic structure of the nonlinear r esonances between the
32: high-frequency oscillations. Our main goal is to make the relations be tween time-averaging
33: eﬀects and smoothness issues more explicit, rather than to obtain global regularity results
34: under minimal restrictions (see, e.g., [5], [7], [14] and the references therein). In particular,

53: investigation.
54: It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
55: also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and

61: Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
62: ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
63: problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
64: we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
65: to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
66: reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
67: in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
68: equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
69: it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
70: similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
71: step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
72: estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
73: the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
74: modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
75: estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can

78: KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
79: one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
80: use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
81: The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
82: terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
83: two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the

88: more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the

5: Abstract. This article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time dis-
6: cretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below H 1. New
7: harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase func-
8: tions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and
9: analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity condi-
10: tions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates
11: of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy
12: techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order γ (up to a
13: logarithmic factor) in L2 under the regularity condition u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ) for γ ∈ (0, 1].

29: 1. Introduction
30: The Korteweg–De Vries (KdV) equation is a nonlinear dispersive partial differential equa-
31: tion that describes many physical phenomena, including shallow water waves, ion acoustic
32: 1
33: 
34: 2
35: waves in plasmas, acoustic waves on crystal lattices, and so on. The development of compu-
36: tational methods for the KdV equation has attracted much attention.
37: It is known that the KdV equation, either on a torus or on the whole space, is globally well-
38: posed in H s with s ≥ 0, i.e., there exists a unique solution in C([0, T]; H s) for any initial value
39: in H s; see [1,10,12,33]. However, classical time discretizations for the KdV equation, including
40: finite difference methods, splitting methods, discontinuous Galerkin methods, and classical
41: exponential integrators, generally require much higher regularity for the numerical solutions
42: to converge with certain orders, i.e., these methods typically require u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3) and
43: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 6) to have first- and second-order convergence in L2, respectively. The error
44: estimates under these regularity conditions (or stronger conditions) for the above-mentioned
45: classical time discretizations have been established, for example, in [7–9, 16, 17, 21, 25, 27, 32].
46: Such regularity conditions are not mere technical conditions required in the error analysis.
47: When the solution of the KdV equation does not have the required regularity, its numerical
48: approximations by the classical time discretizations generally have reduced order of conver-
49: gence.
50: In practice, the solutions of the KdV equation may be rough due to measurement or
51: randomness of the data [2, 5]. To address the numerical approximation to nonsmooth so-
52: lutions, some low-regularity exponential integrators based on resonance analysis were re-
53: cently developed to relax the regularity requirement in solving nonlinear dispersive equations.
54: Such low-regularity integrators based on resonance analysis were initially introduced by Hof-
55: manov´ a & Schratz [6] and Ostermann & Schratz [18, 20] for solving the KdV equation and
56: the nonlinear Schr¨ odinger (NLS) equation, respectively. In particular, for the KdV equa-
57: tion, the low-regularity integrator proposed in [6] can have first-order convergence in H 1 for
58: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3). Wu & Zhao [30] showed that another method outlined in [6] can have
59: second-order convergence in H γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+4) with γ ≥ 0. In a more recent arti-
60: cle, Wu & Zhao [31] proposed two embedded low-regularity integrators for the KdV equation,
61: which have first-order convergence inH γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+1) with γ >1

6: ## Page 2: complete selected statement and standing definitions
7: 
8: Theorem 1 (Logarithm-free convergence), with the standing definitions of Section 2 of the supplied paper.
9: 
10: Use normalized measure dx/(2*pi) on the torus \mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/(2*pi \mathbb{Z}). The Fourier coefficient is
11: \hat f(k)=(2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x) exp(-i*k*x) dx,
12: and ||f||_(H^s)^2=sum_(k in Z) <k>^(2s)|\hat f(k)|^2, where <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2).
13: These spaces are the completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms; negative spaces are interpreted as distributions. The normalized L^2 norm is the s=0 norm. For mean-zero functions, the homogeneous norm uses |k|^(2s) in place of <k>^(2s). For s>=0,
14: ||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s);
15: for s<0, 2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=||f||_(dot H^s).
16: Real-valued means \hat f(-k)=overline(\hat f(k)), and mean-zero means \hat f(0)=0.
17: All time suprema concern continuous representatives; derivative norms are essential suprema.
18: 
19: Let S_t=exp(-t*partial_x^3), so \widehat{S_t f}(k)=exp(i*t*k^3)\hat f(k).
20: Let P_0 be the mean and P=I-P_0. Let D^(-1)=partial_x^(-1) have multiplier (i*k)^(-1) for k!=0 and zero at k=0; D^(-2)=(D^(-1))^2.
21: The equation is
22: u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2),  u(0)=u_0. [Eq. (1)]
23: The exact solution u is the unique real, mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) solution obtained by smooth approximation and satisfies this equation distributionally.
24: 
25: For a positive integer L and tau=T/L, the fixed time-semidiscrete scheme is u^0=u_0 and
26: u^(n+1)=S_tau u^n+F_tau(u^n)+H_tau(u^n), 0<=n<L, [Eq. (2)]
27: where
28: F_tau(f)=(1/6)P[(S_tau D^(-1)f)^2]-(1/6)S_tau P[(D^(-1)f)^2],
29: H_tau(f)=(1/3)P[(S_tau D^(-1)f)D^(-1)F_tau(f)]
30:  +(tau/9)(S_tau D^(-1)f)P_0(f^2)
31:  -(1/54)[S_(tau-s)D^(-1)[(S_s D^(-1)f)^3]]_(s=0)^(s=tau)
32:  -(1/(27*tau))[S_(tau-s)D^(-2)[(S_(s-tau)D^(-2)F_tau(f))(S_s D^(-1)f)]]_(s=0)^(s=tau).
33: Each bracket [G(s)]_(s=0)^(s=tau) means G(tau)-G(0).
34: This is the fixed scheme of the paper's reference [1, Eq. (1.4)], without a spatial frequency cutoff.
35: 
36: For every T>0, every 0<gamma<=1 and every R>0, there exist C>0 and tau_0>0 depending only on T,gamma,R such that, for every real, mean-zero u_0 in H^gamma(\mathbb{T}) with ||u_0||_(H^gamma)<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau_0, this exact fixed scheme satisfies
37: max_(0<=n<=L) ||u(n*tau)-u^n||_(L^2)<=C*tau^gamma.
38: The same C and tau_0 apply to the entire stated initial-data ball; no spectral support bound or additional smoothness is a hypothesis.
39: 
40: In the source's standing notation v(t)=S_(-t)u(t) and M=1+sup_(0<=t<=T)||v(t)||_(H^gamma).
41: Constants C_M may vary from line to line and depend on gamma,T,M, but are uniform in n,tau and spectral support. Section 2.1 supplies M<=1+A(T,gamma,R) uniformly on the ball using the cited exact-flow results; it is not an extra hypothesis on u_0. The source uses the continuous estimates from [1, Proposition 3.4 and Lemma 7.2] and does not use the logarithmic convergence theorem as an input.
42:

44: ## Page 3: original definitions and formulas (3)–(6)
45: 
46: For real alpha,beta,
47: M_tau g=(1/tau) integral_0^tau g(s) ds,
48: eta_tau(alpha,beta)=M_tau(exp(-i*s*(alpha+beta)))-M_tau(exp(-i*s*alpha))*M_tau(exp(-i*s*beta)).
49: For k=a+b+c,
50: p=a+b, alpha=3*a*b*p, beta=3*k*c*p, Phi=alpha+beta=k^3-a^3-b^3-c^3. (3)
51: For k!=0,
52: \widehat{R^n_(2,tau)(f_1,f_2,f_3)}(k)
53:  =-tau/(18*i*k) sum_(a+b+c=k, a+b!=0) exp(-i*t_n*Phi)*eta_tau(alpha,beta)*\hat f_1(a)*\hat f_2(b)*\hat f_3(c), (4)
54: with zero output at k=0. Terms with a zero input frequency vanish because then alpha=0 or beta=0.
55: Lemma 2: if alpha*beta!=0,
56: |eta_tau(alpha,beta)|<=2*min{|alpha/beta|,|beta/alpha|}, (5)
57: |eta_tau(alpha,beta)|<=tau*min{|alpha|,|beta|}. (6)
58: If either phase vanishes, eta_tau=0.

60: ## Pages 4–5: (7)–(11)
61: 
62: For nonzero integers a,b,c,d with a+b+c+d=0, let N_1>=N_2>=N_3>=N_4 be the decreasing rearrangement of their absolute values. N_3 is third largest among all four, including d=-k. N_1<=3*N_2. Put A=|a*b|, B=|c*d|.
63: (1/|d|)*min{A/B,B/A}<=3/N_3. (7)
64: |a+b|/max(A,B)<=6/N_3. (8)
65: For nonnegative x_j in ell^2(Z\{0}),
66: sum_(a+b+c+d=0, a*b*c*d!=0) x_1(a)*x_2(b)*x_3(c)*x_4(d)/N_3(a,b,c,d)
67:  <=C*product_(j=1)^4 ||x_j||_(ell^2). (9)
68: The same conclusion holds after restricting the sum to any subset.
69: 
70: Page 5's shell proof uses 2^j<=|k|<2^(j+1), j>=0, X_(r,j) the ell^2 norm on the jth shell, ordered shell indices j_1>=j_2>=j_3>=j_4, and j_1-j_2<=2 for a nonzero interaction. Its displayed shell bound is
71: sum_(a+b+c+d=0) product_(r=1)^4 x_(r,j_r)
72:  <=C*2^((j_3+j_4)/2)*product_(r=1)^4 X_(r,j_r).
73: After the N_3 weight, the factor is C*2^(-(j_3-j_4)/2). For q=j_1-j_2 in {0,1,2}, the displayed bound is

10: Use normalized measure dx/(2*pi) on the torus \mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/(2*pi \mathbb{Z}). The Fourier coefficient is
11: \hat f(k)=(2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x) exp(-i*k*x) dx,
12: and ||f||_(H^s)^2=sum_(k in Z) <k>^(2s)|\hat f(k)|^2, where <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2).
13: These spaces are the completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms; negative spaces are interpreted as distributions. The normalized L^2 norm is the s=0 norm. For mean-zero functions, the homogeneous norm uses |k|^(2s) in place of <k>^(2s). For s>=0,
14: ||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s);
15: for s<0, 2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=||f||_(dot H^s).
16: Real-valued means \hat f(-k)=overline(\hat f(k)), and mean-zero means \hat f(0)=0.
17: All time suprema concern continuous representatives; derivative norms are essential suprema.

19: Let S_t=exp(-t*partial_x^3), so \widehat{S_t f}(k)=exp(i*t*k^3)\hat f(k).
20: Let P_0 be the mean and P=I-P_0. Let D^(-1)=partial_x^(-1) have multiplier (i*k)^(-1) for k!=0 and zero at k=0; D^(-2)=(D^(-1))^2.

22: u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2),  u(0)=u_0. [Eq. (1)]
23: The exact solution u is the unique real, mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) solution obtained by smooth approximation and satisfies this equation distributionally.

26: u^(n+1)=S_tau u^n+F_tau(u^n)+H_tau(u^n), 0<=n<L, [Eq. (2)]

6: Abstract. In this paper we develop and use successive averaging method s for explaining the regular-
7: ization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg–de Vries (Kd V) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev
8: spaces ˙H s, for s ≥ 0. Speciﬁcally, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous
9: dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the period ic KdV. For the case where the initial data
10: is in L2 we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these so lutions with respect to the initial
11: data as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s, for s ∈ (−1, 0].
12: Keywords: Korteweg–de Vries equation, dispersive equations, averaging met hod, non-
13: linear resonance.

15: 1. Introduction
16: This paper is motivated by works on global regularity of solutions of 3 D problems in
17: hydrodynamics (Navier-Stokes or Boussinesq system with periodic boundary conditions)
18: in the presence of fast rotation or strong stratiﬁcation, see, e.g ., [1], [2], [3], [4], [11],
19: [12], [18], [16], [20], [26], and references therein. The results are base d on the presence of
20: high-frequency waves that lead to destructive interference and eﬀectively weaken the non-
21: linearity through time averaging allowing to prove global regularity of solutions for these
22: problems, at the limit of inﬁnite rotation. The above mentioned hydro dynamical problems
23: are rather complicated (Boussinesq system, for example, involves ﬁve unknown functions of
24: three spatial variables and time, the equations are coupled throug h a quadratic nonlinear-
25: ity). Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to apply this averagin g approach to a slightly
26: simpler problem to make these ideas more transparent. Here we con sider the Korteweg–de
27: Vries equation with one spatial variable subjected to periodic bound ary condition. The
28: averaging eﬀects are strong because on high Fourier modes the line ar term generates high-
29: frequency oscillations which weakens the nonlinearity and makes it mild er. In this paper
30: we show connections between the smoothness properties of solut ions of the Korteweg–de
31: Vries (KdV) equation and the algebraic structure of the nonlinear r esonances between the
32: high-frequency oscillations. Our main goal is to make the relations be tween time-averaging
33: eﬀects and smoothness issues more explicit, rather than to obtain global regularity results
34: under minimal restrictions (see, e.g., [5], [7], [14] and the references therein). In particular,
35: our approach and aim are completely diﬀerent than the machinery an d harmonic analysis

50: diﬀerential equations (see the discussion and references mention ed below). Moreover, we
51: also remark that the tools and ideas that are developed in this contr ibution can be easily
52: applied to multi-dimensional equations and multi-component systems , a subject of future
53: investigation.
54: It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
55: also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and
56: [16] to show that fast rotation prevents the formation of a ﬁnite t ime singularity in the
57: two-dimensional Burgers system. We will use this warmup toy model, and in particular
58: the approach in [1], to ﬁx ideas and to illustrate in section 2 the averag ing mechanism,
59: which is instrumental in regularizing the solutions and in preventing th e formation of a
60: ﬁnite time singularity for the two-dimensional inviscid Burgers syste m.
61: Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
62: ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
63: problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
64: we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
65: to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
66: reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
67: in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
68: equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
69: it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
70: similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
71: step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
72: estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
73: the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
74: modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
75: estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can
76: be easily adjusted to general multidimensional problems such as tho se mentioned above
77: in hydrodynamic problems. We do not use in our analysis the speciﬁc pr operties of the
78: KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
79: one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
80: use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
81: The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
82: terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
83: two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the
84: relevant well-posedness results. In section 4 we use the Galerkin pr ocedure for proving the
85: global existence in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s >0. In section 5 we use the Contraction
86: Principle to show that the solutions established in section 4 are unique and Lipschitz
87: continuous, with respect to the initial data, in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s ≥ 1/2. A
88: more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the
89: case s = 0 is dealt with separately. Finally, for solutions with initial data in L2 we show
90: the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions, with resp ect to the initial data,
91: as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s for all s ∈ (−1, 0].
92: There is a long history of the KdV equations in the periodical setting. We do not attempt
93: to give here a complete survey of this long history, but we are satisﬁ ed by mentioning,
94: below, some of the key landmark results. First Bourgain [6] proved local well-posedness in
95: L2. We observe that the result of Bourgain also implies global existence for the real valued
96: KdV in L2. Later the local well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s > −1/2, was
97:

99: established for the real and complex valued KdV by Kenig, Ponce, an d Vega [14]. Later
100: global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1/2, was established for the real
101: valued KdV by Colliander, Keel, Staﬃlani, Takaoka and Tao [7]. Using th e fact that the
102: KdV equation is an integrable system, and by implementing the inverse method, Kappeler
103: and Topalov [15] proved global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1.
104: Even though the results presented in this contribution are weaker than the state-of-the-
105: art results mentioned above, our approach is substantially diﬀeren t and easy to master.
106: Speciﬁcally, and as we have stressed above, our approach is based on systematic applica-
107: tion of time averaging. It is worth mentioning that since we rewrite th e KdV equation
108: in diﬀerent forms, based on the diﬀerentiation by parts with respec t to the time variable,
109: there is superﬁcial similarity with the reduction to normal forms (cf . [19]). The diﬀerence
110: is that the consecutive forms of the KdV, which we derive, are base d not on the geometric
111: properties such as a reduction to a linear form or a reduction to inva riant tori, but ex-
112: clusively on time averaging properties. In order to stress the eﬀec ts, which are due solely
113: to the time averaging, we do not use energy conservation or modiﬁe d energy functionals
114: as in the I-method. We use only the L2 norm conservation to mimic the situation which
115: occurs in the three-dimensional Euler equations and other hydrod ynamical systems.
116: Moreover, we believe that the averaging approach presented her e can be pushed further
117: to achieve the best known results concerning the KdV equation. Fu rthermore, diﬀerent
118: nonlinear dispersive and wave equations, such as the m-KdV, the Kle in-Gordon equation
119: and water wave equations (see for example, [13], [19], [23]-[25], and re ferences therein),
120: can possibly be studied quite similarly, a subject of future research .

2: FOR THE KDV EQUA TION WITH SOLUTIONS BELOW H1
3: BUYANG LI AND YIFEI WU
4: Communicated by Arieh Iserles
5: Abstract. This article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time dis-
6: cretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below H 1. New
7: harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase func-
8: tions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and
9: analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity condi-
10: tions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates
11: of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy
12: techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order γ (up to a
13: logarithmic factor) in L2 under the regularity condition u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ) for γ ∈ (0, 1].
14: Keywords: KdV equation, rough data, low-regularity integrator, stability, error estimates

29: 1. Introduction
30: The Korteweg–De Vries (KdV) equation is a nonlinear dispersive partial differential equa-
31: tion that describes many physical phenomena, including shallow water waves, ion acoustic
32: 1
33: 
34: 2
35: waves in plasmas, acoustic waves on crystal lattices, and so on. The development of compu-
36: tational methods for the KdV equation has attracted much attention.
37: It is known that the KdV equation, either on a torus or on the whole space, is globally well-
38: posed in H s with s ≥ 0, i.e., there exists a unique solution in C([0, T]; H s) for any initial value
39: in H s; see [1,10,12,33]. However, classical time discretizations for the KdV equation, including
40: finite difference methods, splitting methods, discontinuous Galerkin methods, and classical
41: exponential integrators, generally require much higher regularity for the numerical solutions
42: to converge with certain orders, i.e., these methods typically require u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3) and
43: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 6) to have first- and second-order convergence in L2, respectively. The error
44: estimates under these regularity conditions (or stronger conditions) for the above-mentioned
45: classical time discretizations have been established, for example, in [7–9, 16, 17, 21, 25, 27, 32].
46: Such regularity conditions are not mere technical conditions required in the error analysis.
47: When the solution of the KdV equation does not have the required regularity, its numerical
48: approximations by the classical time discretizations generally have reduced order of conver-
49: gence.
50: In practice, the solutions of the KdV equation may be rough due to measurement or
51: randomness of the data [2, 5]. To address the numerical approximation to nonsmooth so-
52: lutions, some low-regularity exponential integrators based on resonance analysis were re-
53: cently developed to relax the regularity requirement in solving nonlinear dispersive equations.
54: Such low-regularity integrators based on resonance analysis were initially introduced by Hof-
55: manov´ a & Schratz [6] and Ostermann & Schratz [18, 20] for solving the KdV equation and
56: the nonlinear Schr¨ odinger (NLS) equation, respectively. In particular, for the KdV equa-
57: tion, the low-regularity integrator proposed in [6] can have first-order convergence in H 1 for
58: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3). Wu & Zhao [30] showed that another method outlined in [6] can have
59: second-order convergence in H γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+4) with γ ≥ 0. In a more recent arti-
60: cle, Wu & Zhao [31] proposed two embedded low-regularity integrators for the KdV equation,
61: which have first-order convergence inH γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+1) with γ >1
62: 2 and second-order
63: convergence H γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+3) with γ ≥ 0, respectively. The minimal regularity re-
64: quirement for the convergence analysis of these unfiltered algorithms for the KdV equation is
65: u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ) for γ >3/2. This condition naturally arises in the energy type of stability
66: analysis.
67: The convergence of a fully discrete finite difference method was proved in [4] for u ∈
68: C([0, T]; H γ) with γ ≥ 3/4 under the CFL condition ∆ t ≤ ∆x3, where ∆ t and ∆ x denote
69: the stepsize and mesh size in the temporal and spatial discretizations, respectively. The CFL
70: condition in a finite difference method plays a similar role as the filters in a spectral method,
71: i.e., to improve the stability of the method under low-regularity conditions. In the case of
72: γ = 3/4, the method is proved convergent with order 1 /42. Since the convergence analysis
73: relies on the smoothing effect on R, the proof cannot be extended to the torus T.
74: Similarly, the development of low-regularity integrators for the NLS equations can be found
75: in [13, 14, 23, 29]. The minimal regularity requirement for the convergence analysis of the

5888: 11. Conclusions and extended studies
5889: We have presented several new tools for the construction and analysis of low-regularity
5890: integrators for the KdV equations, including the averaging approximation technique for ex-
5891: ponential functions with imaginary powers (Lemma 3.2), the new estimates for the symbol
5892: ϕ = k3 − k3
5893: 1 − k3
5894: 2 − k3
5895: 3 (Lemma 3.3), and new trilinear estimates associated to the KdV op-
5896: erator (Proposition 3.4). These new techniques have played essential roles in analyzing the
5897: local error, global remainder, and the stability estimates. We have also introduced a new
5898: technique, which reformulates the numerical scheme into a perturbed integral formulation of
5899: the continuous KdV equation globally posed on the time interval [0 , T], instead of locally
5900: posed on [tn, tn+1], for analyzing the stability of numerical approximations to solutions below
5901: H 1. By combining the several new techniques, we have constructed a new time discretiza-
5902: tion which is convergent with order γ in L2 (up to a logarithmic factor) under the regularity
5903: condition u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ), with γ ∈ (0, 1] possibly approaching zero.
5904: This paper focuses on the development of low-regularity integrators that could improve
5905: the convergence rates of time discretization without the necessity of using filters. Typically,
5906: filters necessitates a stepsize that correlates with the degrees of freedom in space discretization,
5907: similar to a CFL condition. Our approach increases the flexibility in choosing the degrees of
5908: freedom for space discretization, which enables the design of a fully discrete numerical scheme
5909: that operates independently of any CFL condition. We believe that rigorous analysis of the
5910: full discretization, when coupled with the Fourier spectral method in space, can be conducted
5911: within the theoretical framework proposed in this paper, which provides a foundation for such
5912: future research.
5913: The algorithm constructed in this paper improves the error from O(τ γ/3) to O(τ γ ln(1/τ )),
5914: with a logarithmic factor ln(1 /τ ) arising from technical estimates detailed within our paper.
5915: The optimality of the logarithmic factor ln(1 /τ ) is uncertain since the numerical tests cannot
5916: reveal the logarithmic influence on convergence rates. Typically, if the theoretical error is
5917: expressed as O(τ γ−ϵ) for any ϵ in the range (0 , γ), numerical tests would generally reflect a
5918: convergence order of γ. Hence, further study is required to determine if the logarithmic term
5919: can be refined in future analyses.
5920: The methodologies and theoretical framework introduced in this article can be extended
5921: to develop low-regularity integrators for a variety of nonlinear dispersive equations. These in-
5922: clude the modified KdV equation, the generalized KdV equation, and the nonlinear Schr¨ odinger
5923: (NLS) equation. For instance, consider the NLS equation given by

653: FFT convolution for longer arrays, with no circular aliasing in either path. A step costsO(KlogK )
654: with FFT products andO(K)working storage; retaining allL + 1states costs O(LK). The direct

{"path": "nl0/references/conditional-sources.md", "total_lines": 80, "start": 1, "end": 80, "start_column": 0, "end_column": 63, "requested_end": 220, "has_more": false, "next_start": null, "next_column": 0, "next_end": null, "text": "1: # Explicit continuation with unverified primary sources
2: 
3: Try the actual source before deferring it. Follow [ordered retrieval](source-retrieval.md):
4: arXiv first, Google full text, Google DOI discovery, then Sci-Hub with a confirmed
5: DOI. The author and global reviewer have `search_external_sources` with an
6: explicit engine and `read_external_source` with optional `browser=true`.
7: The controller preserves
8: actual access records and document/text hashes. A search result, HTTP success
9: or readable abstract alone is not theorem verification. Browser-only pages,
10: unresolved challenges, paywalls and access failures are recorded.
11: The invoking agent may use its ordinary source tools or ask for human access
12: when needed, while keeping every supplied document explicit and hash-bound.
13: The reader returns case-relative `evidence` and `primary_evidence_candidates`
14: for downloaded bytes and extracted text. These are readable-source candidates,
15: not a judgment of authenticity: only designate the actual original source as
16: primary, and retain the access record alongside it. PDF staging uses pdftotext
17: when available, otherwise pypdf; neither extraction establishes theorem fidelity.
18: 
19: For JavaScript or verification pages, retry the source tool with `browser=true`.
20: Its trusted helper uses a fresh local Chrome context and ordinary site controls,
21: including the site's own ALTCHA button, without personal cookies or a paid
22: service. Unsupported challenges stay `HUMAN_ACCESS_REQUIRED`; missing browser
23: tools and browser errors remain recorded failures. The invoking agent may use
24: an actual built-in-browser control tool before dispatch; merely opening or
25: queuing a tab is not evidence that results or a paper were read. A downloaded
26: paper can be an explicit source input before dispatch, or part of a new reviewed
27: source revision. Never change an active run's frozen input files to insert a
28: browser result. The isolated CLI stages do not control the user's desktop tabs.
29: 
30: If the primary text remains unavailable, continue only from a complete external
31: statement actually present in a supplied secondary source. Call
32: `defer_primary_source` with its E ID, exact statement/quotation, input ID and
33: own failed access-record paths. No missing theorem may be invented from model
34: memory. Known contradictions remain failures, not access deferrals.
35: 
36: The tool returns `verification: {status: UNVERIFIED_PRIMARY, record: {path,
37: sha256}}`. Put it in `E.source`, use empty `primary_evidence`, and retain the
38: normal author/title/version/locator/context fields with honest uncertainty.
39: The author contract binds the supporting secondary text and access records.
40: The statement must preserve the quotation. This is an explicit assumption for
41: conditional work; neither a familiar name nor a lookup failure proves it.
42: 
43: ## Review and continuation boundaries
44: 
45: Global Audit A keeps the E review and unavailable primary citation checks
46: `UNVERIFIED`. It must still examine whether the explicit secondary statement is
47: complete and whether its declared role is legitimate. Every other mathematical
48: check, every local R check and every external application must actually PASS.
49: Source-only findings may be UNVERIFIED at that E's source location. A FAIL,
50: an unassessed item, unrelated uncertainty or an incomplete statement prevents
51: conditional continuation. A deferred source can never receive a verified PASS
52: until its source record is replaced and the affected checks are actually done.
53: 
54: The machine result has `current_standard_receipt_valid: false` and, only when
55: these conditions hold, `current_conditional_receipt_valid: true`. The ordinary
56: receipt and every unresolved judgment stay intact. The same exact source/A
57: is used in translation; optional source factoring is skipped for this route.
58: Local Lean proofs, assembly and native trust checks still have to complete.
59: Audit B compares Lean external premises with the explicit frozen E statements
60: and checks the entire target. It does not reclassify the unverified publication
61: claims as verified. Upstream source uncertainty remains attached to the result.
62: 
63: Final states are `DRAFT-AUDIT-CONDITIONAL`, `AUDIT-B-CONDITIONAL`, or
64: `WORKFLOW-CONDITIONAL`. They are distinct from ordinary PASS. The execution may
65: finish normally, but `acceptance_target_satisfied` remains false and source
66: follow-up remains required. Other failed mathematics cannot use this route.
67: 
68: ## User notification
69: 
70: At invocation, explain that inaccessible primary sources can lead to a
71: conditional result, not full source verification. When an actual source is
72: deferred, display its warning and the remaining check in progress/status.
73: Do not wait for the user to discover an internal JSON file.
74: 
75: The source and final run retain `warn.json` and `warn.md`: original target and
76: source hashes, E IDs, exact assumed statements, actual retrieval-record links,
77: and the meaning of the remaining uncertainty. Include these files and a plain
78: language qualification in the final response. A Lean build does not remove
79: these warnings. New verification requires actual primary readback and fresh
80: affected review, never a manual change from UNVERIFIED to PASS."}

{"path": "nl0/references/logical-rules.md", "total_lines": 78, "start": 1, "end": 78, "start_column": 0, "end_column": 75, "requested_end": 200, "has_more": false, "next_start": null, "next_column": 0, "next_end": null, "text": "1: # Package local reasoning as true theorem nodes
2: 
3: The main graph has only E/M/H source propositions. A temporary assumption is
4: an argument-local device, never a trusted graph vertex. Every exported N/P is
5: a complete claim under the frozen original context. The audit inspects the
6: local derivation; surface implication syntax alone is insufficient.
7: The complete [neutral JSON example](../templates/quantified-implication-example.md)
8: shows an arbitrary binder, a local antecedent, its discharge and the full
9: quantified output. Follow this accounting rather than silently granting a
10: property in a local object's type.
11: 
12: ## Implication and contradiction
13: 
14: To prove `X -> Y`, introduce X inside one argument, derive Y from the declared
15: inputs, then discharge X into the antecedent. Output `X -> Y`, not Y. To use Y
16: unconditionally later, supply an actually proved X and apply implication
17: elimination. A local X and a proved X are not the same proof object.
18: 
19: To prove `not X`, derive false under local X and discharge X by negation
20: introduction. To prove P by classical contradiction, first produce the complete
21: theorem `not P -> false` (equivalently `not not P`), then apply the fixed
22: classical rule. A single R may combine the operations if every local assumption
23: is accounted for. No classical double-negation elimination under an
24: intuitionistic-only policy.
25: 
26: Example graph: N1 `(not P -> Q)`, N2 `not Q`, R1 outputs N3
27: `(not P -> false)`, R2 outputs P. The argument of R1 locally assumes not P,
28: applies N1 and N2, and closes that assumption. No `not P` root is added.
29: The fallacy “assume P, obtain P, discharge and output P” fails: its valid output
30: would be `P -> P`.
31: 
32: ## Cases
33: 
34: From an already proved `A or B or C`, obtain a common target Q by complete
35: conditional lemmas `A -> Q`, `B -> Q`, `C -> Q`, then disjunction elimination.
36: Alternatively prove `not A`, `not B` and conclude C using the original
37: disjunction. Eliminating A/B without a proved exhaustive disjunction cannot
38: establish C. A branch producing false can produce the common target by false
39: elimination; it does not make false an unconditional source proposition.
40: 
41: Proof bodies may contain all branches locally instead of exporting every
42: branch lemma. Check coverage, identical target/ambient context, and the absence
43: of sibling-branch fact/witness leakage. Introduce/discharge each branch-local
44: assumption in its actual scope.
45: 
46: ## Quantifiers, witnesses, and induction
47: 
48: For universal introduction use an arbitrary variable, then close its binder.
49: It must not occur free in an undischarged extra assumption. If the intended
50: theorem has a premise H(x), retain it in the quantified implication.
51: 
52: For existential elimination start from a proved existence statement, choose a
53: fresh local witness with exactly its stated properties, and prove a conclusion
54: independent of that witness's private identity. A witness depending on n does
55: not yield one witness valid for every n. Do not turn a local witness into a
56: globally available constant without a legitimate, recorded construction.
57: 
58: For natural-number induction prove the base and the complete step
59: `forall n, Q(n) -> Q(n+1)` and use induction to conclude `forall n, Q(n)`.
60: The induction hypothesis is local to the step; there is no circular graph edge.
61: If the step invokes the hypothesis at a transformed point s, include
62: `forall s` in the induction invariant. Well-founded induction needs the exact
63: well-founded relation/decrease justification; the word “induct” is not enough.
64: 
65: ## Local notation
66: 
67: Global symbols are reserved. Local binders can repeat across separate nodes
68: or separate binding scopes in a node, but cannot shadow a global symbol.
69: `sum_{k=1}^N` binds k only in that expression. Source theorem dummy variables
70: are alpha-renamed locally, not registered as a new global object each time.
71: Freshness, witness dependencies, constant uniformity, and binder scope are
72: mathematical audit obligations; a list of names does not verify the formula.
73: In v2, local declarations identify introduction kind/basis and inclusive S
74: start/end positions. An input-bound name needs instantiation; a witness needs
75: an actual existence premise. Local F facts record their complete statement,
76: statement-local binders, used objects and remaining assumptions. Neither a
77: fact nor a chosen witness may escape its scope. The checker accounts for
78: declared scopes; Audit A must also inspect the actual quantifier reasoning."}

{"path": "nl0/references/conditional-sources.md", "total_lines": 80, "start": 1, "end": 80, "start_column": 0, "end_column": 63, "requested_end": 220, "has_more": false, "next_start": null, "next_column": 0, "next_end": null, "text": "1: # Explicit continuation with unverified primary sources
2: 
3: Try the actual source before deferring it. Follow [ordered retrieval](source-retrieval.md):
4: arXiv first, Google full text, Google DOI discovery, then Sci-Hub with a confirmed
5: DOI. The author and global reviewer have `search_external_sources` with an
6: explicit engine and `read_external_source` with optional `browser=true`.
7: The controller preserves
8: actual access records and document/text hashes. A search result, HTTP success
9: or readable abstract alone is not theorem verification. Browser-only pages,
10: unresolved challenges, paywalls and access failures are recorded.
11: The invoking agent may use its ordinary source tools or ask for human access
12: when needed, while keeping every supplied document explicit and hash-bound.
13: The reader returns case-relative `evidence` and `primary_evidence_candidates`
14: for downloaded bytes and extracted text. These are readable-source candidates,
15: not a judgment of authenticity: only designate the actual original source as
16: primary, and retain the access record alongside it. PDF staging uses pdftotext
17: when available, otherwise pypdf; neither extraction establishes theorem fidelity.
18: 
19: For JavaScript or verification pages, retry the source tool with `browser=true`.
20: Its trusted helper uses a fresh local Chrome context and ordinary site controls,
21: including the site's own ALTCHA button, without personal cookies or a paid
22: service. Unsupported challenges stay `HUMAN_ACCESS_REQUIRED`; missing browser
23: tools and browser errors remain recorded failures. The invoking agent may use
24: an actual built-in-browser control tool before dispatch; merely opening or
25: queuing a tab is not evidence that results or a paper were read. A downloaded
26: paper can be an explicit source input before dispatch, or part of a new reviewed
27: source revision. Never change an active run's frozen input files to insert a
28: browser result. The isolated CLI stages do not control the user's desktop tabs.
29: 
30: If the primary text remains unavailable, continue only from a complete external
31: statement actually present in a supplied secondary source. Call
32: `defer_primary_source` with its E ID, exact statement/quotation, input ID and
33: own failed access-record paths. No missing theorem may be invented from model
34: memory. Known contradictions remain failures, not access deferrals.
35: 
36: The tool returns `verification: {status: UNVERIFIED_PRIMARY, record: {path,
37: sha256}}`. Put it in `E.source`, use empty `primary_evidence`, and retain the
38: normal author/title/version/locator/context fields with honest uncertainty.
39: The author contract binds the supporting secondary text and access records.
40: The statement must preserve the quotation. This is an explicit assumption for
41: conditional work; neither a familiar name nor a lookup failure proves it.
42: 
43: ## Review and continuation boundaries
44: 
45: Global Audit A keeps the E review and unavailable primary citation checks
46: `UNVERIFIED`. It must still examine whether the explicit secondary statement is
47: complete and whether its declared role is legitimate. Every other mathematical
48: check, every local R check and every external application must actually PASS.
49: Source-only findings may be UNVERIFIED at that E's source location. A FAIL,
50: an unassessed item, unrelated uncertainty or an incomplete statement prevents
51: conditional continuation. A deferred source can never receive a verified PASS
52: until its source record is replaced and the affected checks are actually done.
53: 
54: The machine result has `current_standard_receipt_valid: false` and, only when
55: these conditions hold, `current_conditional_receipt_valid: true`. The ordinary
56: receipt and every unresolved judgment stay intact. The same exact source/A
57: is used in translation; optional source factoring is skipped for this route.
58: Local Lean proofs, assembly and native trust checks still have to complete.
59: Audit B compares Lean external premises with the explicit frozen E statements
60: and checks the entire target. It does not reclassify the unverified publication
61: claims as verified. Upstream source uncertainty remains attached to the result.
62: 
63: Final states are `DRAFT-AUDIT-CONDITIONAL`, `AUDIT-B-CONDITIONAL`, or
64: `WORKFLOW-CONDITIONAL`. They are distinct from ordinary PASS. The execution may
65: finish normally, but `acceptance_target_satisfied` remains false and source
66: follow-up remains required. Other failed mathematics cannot use this route.
67: 
68: ## User notification
69: 
70: At invocation, explain that inaccessible primary sources can lead to a
71: conditional result, not full source verification. When an actual source is
72: deferred, display its warning and the remaining check in progress/status.
73: Do not wait for the user to discover an internal JSON file.
74: 
75: The source and final run retain `warn.json` and `warn.md`: original target and
76: source hashes, E IDs, exact assumed statements, actual retrieval-record links,
77: and the meaning of the remaining uncertainty. Include these files and a plain
78: language qualification in the final response. A Lean build does not remove
79: these warnings. New verification requires actual primary readback and fresh
80: affected review, never a manual change from UNVERIFIED to PASS."}

{"path": "nl0/references/logical-rules.md", "total_lines": 78, "start": 1, "end": 78, "start_column": 0, "end_column": 75, "requested_end": 200, "has_more": false, "next_start": null, "next_column": 0, "next_end": null, "text": "1: # Package local reasoning as true theorem nodes
2: 
3: The main graph has only E/M/H source propositions. A temporary assumption is
4: an argument-local device, never a trusted graph vertex. Every exported N/P is
5: a complete claim under the frozen original context. The audit inspects the
6: local derivation; surface implication syntax alone is insufficient.
7: The complete [neutral JSON example](../templates/quantified-implication-example.md)
8: shows an arbitrary binder, a local antecedent, its discharge and the full
9: quantified output. Follow this accounting rather than silently granting a
10: property in a local object's type.
11: 
12: ## Implication and contradiction
13: 
14: To prove `X -> Y`, introduce X inside one argument, derive Y from the declared
15: inputs, then discharge X into the antecedent. Output `X -> Y`, not Y. To use Y
16: unconditionally later, supply an actually proved X and apply implication
17: elimination. A local X and a proved X are not the same proof object.
18: 
19: To prove `not X`, derive false under local X and discharge X by negation
20: introduction. To prove P by classical contradiction, first produce the complete
21: theorem `not P -> false` (equivalently `not not P`), then apply the fixed
22: classical rule. A single R may combine the operations if every local assumption
23: is accounted for. No classical double-negation elimination under an
24: intuitionistic-only policy.
25: 
26: Example graph: N1 `(not P -> Q)`, N2 `not Q`, R1 outputs N3
27: `(not P -> false)`, R2 outputs P. The argument of R1 locally assumes not P,
28: applies N1 and N2, and closes that assumption. No `not P` root is added.
29: The fallacy “assume P, obtain P, discharge and output P” fails: its valid output
30: would be `P -> P`.
31: 
32: ## Cases
33: 
34: From an already proved `A or B or C`, obtain a common target Q by complete
35: conditional lemmas `A -> Q`, `B -> Q`, `C -> Q`, then disjunction elimination.
36: Alternatively prove `not A`, `not B` and conclude C using the original
37: disjunction. Eliminating A/B without a proved exhaustive disjunction cannot
38: establish C. A branch producing false can produce the common target by false
39: elimination; it does not make false an unconditional source proposition.
40: 
41: Proof bodies may contain all branches locally instead of exporting every
42: branch lemma. Check coverage, identical target/ambient context, and the absence
43: of sibling-branch fact/witness leakage. Introduce/discharge each branch-local
44: assumption in its actual scope.
45: 
46: ## Quantifiers, witnesses, and induction
47: 
48: For universal introduction use an arbitrary variable, then close its binder.
49: It must not occur free in an undischarged extra assumption. If the intended
50: theorem has a premise H(x), retain it in the quantified implication.
51: 
52: For existential elimination start from a proved existence statement, choose a
53: fresh local witness with exactly its stated properties, and prove a conclusion
54: independent of that witness's private identity. A witness depending on n does
55: not yield one witness valid for every n. Do not turn a local witness into a
56: globally available constant without a legitimate, recorded construction.
57: 
58: For natural-number induction prove the base and the complete step
59: `forall n, Q(n) -> Q(n+1)` and use induction to conclude `forall n, Q(n)`.
60: The induction hypothesis is local to the step; there is no circular graph edge.
61: If the step invokes the hypothesis at a transformed point s, include
62: `forall s` in the induction invariant. Well-founded induction needs the exact
63: well-founded relation/decrease justification; the word “induct” is not enough.
64: 
65: ## Local notation
66: 
67: Global symbols are reserved. Local binders can repeat across separate nodes
68: or separate binding scopes in a node, but cannot shadow a global symbol.
69: `sum_{k=1}^N` binds k only in that expression. Source theorem dummy variables
70: are alpha-renamed locally, not registered as a new global object each time.
71: Freshness, witness dependencies, constant uniformity, and binder scope are
72: mathematical audit obligations; a list of names does not verify the formula.
73: In v2, local declarations identify introduction kind/basis and inclusive S
74: start/end positions. An input-bound name needs instantiation; a witness needs
75: an actual existence premise. Local F facts record their complete statement,
76: statement-local binders, used objects and remaining assumptions. Neither a
77: fact nor a chosen witness may escape its scope. The checker accounts for
78: declared scopes; Audit A must also inspect the actual quantifier reasoning."}

    Title:On the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries equation

    Authors:Anatoli V. Babin, Alexei A. Ilyin, Edriss S. Titi
            View a PDF of the paper titled On the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries equation, by Anatoli V. Babin and 1 other authors

    View PDF
    HTML (experimental)



    
            Abstract:In this paper we develop and use successive averaging methods for explaining the regularization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg--de Vries (KdV) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev spaces $\dot{H}^s$, for $s\ge0$. Specifically, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the periodic KdV. For the case where the initial data is in $L_2$ we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions with respect to the initial data as maps from $\dot{H}^s$ to $\dot{H}^s$, for $s\in(-1,0]$.

                    Abstract
This article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time discretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below \(H^1\). New harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase functions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity conditions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order \(\gamma \) (up to a logarithmic factor) in \(L^2\) under the regularity condition \(u\in C([0,T];H^\gamma )\) for \(\gamma \in (0,1]\).

D003.notes: The weighted completion, normalized L2, reality conjugation, and zero mode are explicit. The lost conjugation bar in plain extraction is resolved by the supplied checked transcription.

D004.notes: The homogeneous norm is restricted to mean-zero inputs. Both comparison inequalities, including the reversed factors for negative s, follow termwise from 1<=<k>/|k|<=sqrt(2).

D005.notes: The sign exp(i*t*k^3) matches exp(-t*partial_x^3); group composition and norm preservation follow directly from the multiplier, including on completions.

D006.notes: The zeroth distributional Fourier coefficient is a scalar identified with the corresponding constant function; no mean-zero assumption is introduced.

D007.notes: I-P0 defines precisely the complementary mean-zero projection; its dependency is D006.

D008.notes: The zero mode is explicitly assigned zero, so there is no division by zero. The nonzero multipliers give the stated one- and two-derivative gains since <k>/|k|<=sqrt(2).

D009.notes: The guarded tau>0, mean-zero L2 formula is exactly the fixed quadratic stage. Dinv f is H1, hence its square is well-defined and L2 (indeed H1) in one dimension.

D010.notes: All four terms, constants, signs, inverse derivatives, time arguments and endpoint subtraction match the original. For L2 inputs, Dinv f is H1, f^2 is L1, and the displayed smoothed products and mean exist; tau>0 guards 1/tau. No estimate or endpoint identity is assumed.

D011.notes: The unchanged Psi and finite recursion have the original grid, twisting and positive timestep guard. L2 products are defined by D009-D010; continuity and preservation are exported separately in N007 rather than assumed. No frequency cutoff is inserted.

D012.notes: The cutoff and complementary projection are defined for N>=0 on Fourier coefficients. They are explicitly proof/approximation devices, not part of Psi.

D013.notes: An integrable scalar time function and tau>0 suffice for the stated average; the divisor is guarded.

D014.notes: Both phase averages and their product are explicit with real phases and positive tau. Exponentials are integrable; no covariance estimate is granted by the definition.

D015.notes: The nonzero-output guard, omitted pair sum, phase identity, factor -tau/(18*i*k), and time phase exactly match (4). The polynomial core needs no convergence assumption; the smooth-input series is absolutely convergent by |eta|<=2 and rapidly decreasing coefficients. The rough bounded extension is correctly left to N004.

D016.notes: 23/14 is a fixed positive rational, strictly greater than 3/2; it is not a new hypothesis on problem data.

D017.notes: The interval length, weak derivative codomain, essential suprema and X norm match the original. Continuous representatives are used only where continuity is supplied, not postulated for all L-infinity paths.

D018.notes: The twisted derivative-of-product defines B on smooth inputs and, for its actual L2 uses, on L1 products distributionally. The H^(-23/14) bound is an exported N005 conclusion, not a defining axiom.

D019.notes: The normal-form product has the correct two inverse derivatives and output projection. D020.notes: Both projections, the placement of the inverse derivative and time integral match the original. Initial smooth/piecewise smooth inputs make the construction legitimate; rough extensions are supplied by explicit estimates and sources, not hidden in D020.

D021.notes: The bilinear stage has factor 1/2, time-independent smooth mean-zero inputs and a<=t. The subsequent extension and bounds are separate conclusions.
